entries.07ee1f0f5b840daff67d46496d012abb1c6f08a5: <div sID="gen5009" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="Judg.17" sID="Judg.17"/> <div eID="gen5009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5010" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5011" type="x-p"/> All agree that what is related in this and the rest of the chapters to the end of this book was not done, as the narrative occurs, after Samson, but long before, even soon after the death of Joshua, in the days of Phinehas the son of Eleazar, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.28">ch. xx. 28</reference>. But it is cast here into the latter part of the book that it might not interrupt the history of the Judges. That it might appear how happy the nation was in the judges it is here shown how unhappy they were when there was none. I. Then idolatry began in the family of Micah, <reference osisRef="Judg.17.1-Judg.17.13">ch. xvii</reference>. II. Then it spread itself into the tribe of Dan, <reference osisRef="Judg.18.1-Judg.18.31">ch. xviii</reference>. III. Then villany was committed in Gibeah of Benjamin, <reference osisRef="Judg.19.1-Judg.19.30">ch. xix</reference>. IV. Then that whole tribe was destroyed for countenancing it, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.1-Judg.20.48">ch. xx</reference>. V. Then strange expedients were adopted to keep up that tribe, <reference osisRef="Judg.21.1-Judg.21.25">ch. xxi</reference>. Therefore blessed be God for the government we are under! In this chapter we are told how Micah an Ephraimite furnished himself, 1. With an image for his god, <reference osisRef="Judg.17.1-Judg.17.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. 2. With a Levite, such a one as he was, for his priest, <reference osisRef="Judg.17.7-Judg.17.13">ver. 7-13</reference>.
entries.9b43ed2e832e0989fdd9be4798a10001a618785f: <div eID="gen5011" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5010" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Micah and His Gods. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1406.)</title> <div sID="gen5012" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And there was a man of mount Ephraim, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.2">Micah.   2</reference> And he said unto his mother, The eleven hundred <hi type="italic">shekels</hi> of silver that were taken from thee, about which thou cursedst, and spakest of also in mine ears, behold, the silver <hi type="italic">is</hi> with me; I took it. And his mother said, Blessed <hi type="italic">be thou</hi> of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , my son. <hi type="super">3</hi> And when he had restored the eleven hundred <hi type="italic">shekels</hi> of silver to his mother, his mother said, I had wholly dedicated the silver unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> from my hand for my son, to make a graven image and a molten image: now therefore I will restore it unto thee. <hi type="super">4</hi> Yet he restored the money unto his mother; and his mother took two hundred <hi type="italic">shekels</hi> of silver, and gave them to the founder, who made thereof a graven image and a molten image: and they were in the house of <reference osisRef="Mic.5">Micah.   5</reference> And the man Micah had a house of gods, and made an ephod, and teraphim, and consecrated one of his sons, who became his priest. <hi type="super">6</hi> In those days <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no king in Israel, <hi type="italic">but</hi> every man did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> right in his own eyes. <div eID="gen5012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5013" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. Micah and his mother quarrelling. 1. The son robs the mother. The old woman had hoarded, with long scraping and saving, a great sum of money, 1100 pieces of silver. It is likely she intended, when she died, to leave it to her son: in the mean time it did her good to look upon it, and to count it over. The young man had a family of children grown up, for he had one of age to be a priest, <reference osisRef="Judg.17.5">v. 5</reference>. He knows where to find his mother's cash, thinks he has more need of it than she has, cannot stay till she dies, and so takes it away privately for his own use. Though it is a fault in parents to withhold from their children that which is meet, and lead them into temptation to wish them in their graves, yet even this will by no means excuse the wickedness of those children that steal from their parents, and think all their own that they can get from them, though by the most indirect methods. 2. The mother curses the son, or whoever had taken her money. It should seem she suspected her son; for, when she cursed, she spoke in his ears so loud, and with so much passion and vehemence, as made both his ears to tingle. See what mischief the love of money makes, how it destroys the duty and comfort of every relation. It was the love of money that made Micah so undutiful to his mother as to rob her, and made her so unkind and void of natural affection to her son as to curse him if he had it and concealed it. Outward losses drive good people to their prayers, but bad people to their curses. This woman's silver was her god before it was made thither into a graven or a molten image, else the loss of it would not have put her into such a passion as caused her quite to forget and break through all the laws of decency and piety. It is a very foolish thing for those that are provoked to throw their curses about <hi type="italic">as a madman that casteth fire-brands, arrows, and death,</hi> since they know not but they may light upon those that are most dear to them. <div eID="gen5013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5014" type="x-p"/> II. Micah and his mother reconciled. 1. The son was so terrified with his mother's curses that he restored the money. Though he had so little grace as to take it, he had so much left as not to dare to keep it when his mother had sent a curse after it. He cannot believe his mother's money will do him any good without his mother's blessing, nor dares he deny the theft when he is charged with it, nor retain the money when it is demanded by the right owner. It is best not to do evil, but it is next best, when it is done, to undo it again by repentance, confession, and restitution. Let children be afraid of having the prayers of their parents against them; for, though the curse causeless shall not come, yet that which is justly deserved may be justly feared, even though it was passionately and indecently uttered. 2. The mother was so pleased with her son's repentance that she recalled her curses, and turned them into prayers for her son's welfare: <hi type="italic">Blessed be thou of the Lord, my son.</hi> When those that have been guilty of a fault appear to be free and ingenuous in owning it they ought to be commended for their repentance, rather than still be condemned and upbraided for their fault. <div eID="gen5014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5015" type="x-p"/> III. Micah and his mother agreeing to turn their money into a god, and set up idolatry in their family; and this seems to have been the first instance of the revolt of any Israelite from God and his instituted worship after the death of Joshua and the elders that out-lived him, and is therefore thus particularly related. And though this was only the worship of the true God by an image, against the <hi type="italic">second</hi> commandment, yet this opened the door to the worship of other gods, Baalim and the groves, against the <hi type="italic">first and great</hi> commandment. Observe, <div eID="gen5015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5016" type="x-p"/> 1. The mother's contrivance of this matter. When the silver was restored she pretended she had <hi type="italic">dedicated it to the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.17.3">v. 3</reference>), either before it was stolen, and then she would have this thought to be the reason why she was so much grieved at the loss of it and imprecated evil on him that had taken it, because it was a dedicated and therefore an accursed thing, or after it was stolen she had made a vow that, if she could retrieve it, she would dedicate it to God, and then she would have the providence that had so far favoured her as to bring it back to her hands to be an owning of her vow. "Come," said she to her son, "the money is mine, but thou hast a mind to it; let it be neither mine nor thine, but let us both agree to make it into an image for a religious use." Had she put it to a use that was indeed for the service and honour of God, this would have been a good way of accommodating the matter between them; but, as it was, the project was wicked. Probably this old woman was one of those that came out of Egypt, and would have such images made as she had seen there; now that she began to dote she called to remembrance the follies of her youth, and perhaps told her son that this way of worshipping God by images was, to her knowledge, the old religion. <div eID="gen5016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5017" type="x-p"/> 2. The son's compliance with her. It should seem, when she first proposed the thing he stumbled at it, knowing what the second commandment was; for, when she said (<reference osisRef="Judg.17.3">v. 3</reference>) she designed it for her son to make an image of, yet he restored it to his mother (being loth to have a hand in making the image), and she gave it to the founder and had the thing done, blaming him perhaps for scrupling at it, <reference osisRef="Judg.17.4">v. 4</reference>. But, when the images were made, Micah, by his mother's persuasion, was not only well reconciled to them, but greatly pleased and in love with them; so strangely bewitching was idolatry, and so much supported by <hi type="italic">traditions received from their parents,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1 Pet. i. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jer. xliv. 17</reference>. But observe how the old woman's covetousness prevailed, in part, above her superstition. She had wholly dedicated the silver to make the graven and molten images (<reference osisRef="Judg.17.3">v. 3</reference>), all the 1100 pieces; but, when it came to be done, she made less than a fifth part serve, even 200 <hi type="italic">shekels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.17.4">v. 4</reference>. She thought that enough, and indeed it was too much to give for an image that is a teacher of lies. Had it been devoted truly to the honour of God, he would not thus have been put off with part of the price, but would have signified his resentment of the affront, as he did in the case of Ananias and Sapphira. Now observe, <div eID="gen5017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5018" type="x-p"/> (1.) What was the corruption here introduced, <reference osisRef="Judg.17.5">v. 5</reference>. The man Micah had <hi type="italic">a house of gods, a house of God,</hi> so the LXX., for so he thought it, as good as that at Shiloh, and better, because his own, of his own inventing and at his own disposal; for people love to have their religion under their girdle, to manage it as they please. <hi type="italic">A house of error,</hi> so the Chaldee, for really it was so, a deviation from the way of truth and an inlet to all deceit. Idolatry is a great cheat, and one of the worst of errors. That which he aimed at in the progress of his idolatry, whether he designed it at first or no, was to mimic and rival both God's oracles and his ordinances. [1.] His oracles; for he made <hi type="italic">teraphim,</hi> little images which he might advise with as there was occasion, and receive informations, directions, and predictions from. What the <hi type="italic">urim</hi> and <hi type="italic">thummim</hi> were to the prince and people these <hi type="italic">teraphim</hi> should be to his family; yet he could not think that the true God would own them, or give answers by them, and therefore depended upon such demons as the heathen worshipped to inspire them and make them serviceable to him. Thus, while the honour of Jehovah was pretended (<reference osisRef="Judg.17.3">v. 3</reference>), yet, his institution being relinquished, these Israelites unavoidably lapsed into downright idolatry and demon-worship. [2.] His ordinances. Some room or apartment in the house of Micah was appointed for the temple or house of God; an ephod, or holy garment, was provided for his priest to officiate in, in imitation of those used at the tabernacle of God, and one of his sons he consecrated, probably the eldest, to be his priest. And, when he had set up a graven or molten image to represent the object of his worship, no marvel if a priest of his own getting and his own making served to be the manager of it. Here is no mention of any altar, sacrifice, or incense, in honour of these silver gods, but, having a priest, it is probable he had all these, unless we suppose that, at first, his gods were intended only to be advised with, not to be adored, like Laban's teraphim; but the beginning of idolatry, as of other sins, is <hi type="italic">like the letting forth of water:</hi> break the dam, and you bring a deluge. Here idolatry began, and it spread like a fretting leprosy. Dr. Lightfoot would have us observe that as 1100 pieces of silver were here devoted to the making of an idol, which ruined religion, especially in the tribe of Dan (as we shall presently find), which was Samson's tribe, so 1100 pieces of silver were given by each Philistine lord for the ruin of Samson. <div eID="gen5018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5019" type="x-p"/> (2.) What was the cause of this corruption (<reference osisRef="Judg.17.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">There was no king in Israel,</hi> no judge or sovereign prince to take cognizance of the setting up of these images (which, doubtless, the country about soon resorted to), and to give orders for the destroying of them, none to convince Micah of his error and to restrain and punish him, to take this disease in time, by which the spreading of the infection might have been happily prevented. Every man did that which was <hi type="italic">right in his own eyes,</hi> and then they soon did that which was <hi type="italic">evil in the sight of the Lord.</hi> When they were without a king to keep good order among them, God's house was forsaken, his priests were neglected, and all went to ruin among them. See what a mercy government is, and what reason there is that not only <hi type="italic">prayers and intercessions, but giving of thanks,</hi> should <hi type="italic">be made for kings and all in authority,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1-1Tim.2.2">1 Tim. ii. 1, 2</reference>. Nothing contributes more, under God, to the support of religion in the world, than the due administration of those two great ordinances, magistracy and ministry.
entries.e97bd9a11377e13c4f95b5e50d85ab1e72b55613: <div eID="gen5019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5020" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And there was a young man out of Beth-lehem-judah of the family of Judah, who <hi type="italic">was</hi> a Levite, and he sojourned there. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the man departed out of the city from Beth-lehem-judah to sojourn where he could find <hi type="italic">a place:</hi> and he came to mount Ephraim to the house of Micah, as he journeyed. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Micah said unto him, Whence comest thou? And he said unto him, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a Levite of Beth-lehem-judah, and I go to sojourn where I may find <hi type="italic">a place.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> And Micah said unto him, Dwell with me, and be unto me a father and a priest, and I will give thee ten <hi type="italic">shekels</hi> of silver by the year, and a suit of apparel, and thy victuals. So the Levite went in. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the Levite was content to dwell with the man; and the young man was unto him as one of his sons. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Micah consecrated the Levite; and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of <reference osisRef="Mic.13">Micah.   13</reference> Then said Micah, Now know I that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to <hi type="italic">my</hi> priest. <div eID="gen5020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5021" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of Micah's furnishing himself with a Levite for his chaplain, either thinking his son, because the heir of his estate, too good to officiate, or rather, because not of God's tribe, not good enough. Observe, <div eID="gen5021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5022" type="x-p"/> I. What brought this Levite to Micah. By his mother's side he was of the family of Judah, and lived at Bethlehem among his mother's relations (for that was not a Levites' city), or, upon some other account, as a stranger or inmate, sojourned there, <reference osisRef="Judg.17.7">v. 7</reference>. Thence he went to <hi type="italic">sojourn where he could find a place,</hi> and in his travels came to the house of Micah in Mount Ephraim, <reference osisRef="Judg.17.8">v. 8</reference>. Now, 1. Some think it was his unhappiness that he was under a necessity of removing, either because he was persecuted and abused, or rather neglected and starved, at Bethlehem. God had made plentiful provision for the Levites, but the people withheld their dues, and did not help them into the possession of the cities assigned to them; so that they were reduced to straits, and no care was taken for their relief. Israel's forsaking God began with forsaking the Levites, which therefore they are warned against, <reference osisRef="Deut.12.19">Deut. xii. 19</reference>. It is a sign religion is going to decay when good ministers are neglected and at a loss for a livelihood. But, 2. It seems rather to have been his fault and folly, that he loved to wander, threw himself out where he was, and forfeited the respect of his friends, and, having a roving head, would go to seek his fortune, as we say. We cannot conceive that things had yet come to such a pass among them that a Levite should be poor, unless it was his own fault. As those are fit to be pitied that would fix but may not, so those are fit to be punished that might fix but will not. Unsettledness being, one would think, a constant uneasiness, it is strange that any Israelite, especially any Levite, should affect it. <div eID="gen5022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5023" type="x-p"/> II. What bargain Micah made with him. Had he not been well enough content with his son for his priest, he would have gone or sent abroad to enquire out a Levite, but now he only takes hold of one that drops into his hands, which showed that he had no great zeal in the matter. It is probable that this rambling Levite had heard, in the country, of Micah's house of <hi type="italic">gods, his graven and molten image,</hi> which, if he had had any thing of the spirit of a Levite in him, would have brought him thither to reprove Micah for his idolatry, to tell how directly contrary it was to the law of God, and how it would bring the judgments of God upon him; but instead of this, like a base and degenerate branch of that sacred tribe, thither he goes to offer his service, with, <hi type="italic">Have you any work for a Levite?</hi> for I am out of business, and <hi type="italic">go to sojourn where I may find a place;</hi> all he aimed at was to get bread, not to do good, <reference osisRef="Judg.17.9">v. 9</reference>. Micah courts him into his family (<reference osisRef="Judg.17.10">v. 10</reference>), and promises him, 1. Good preferment: <hi type="italic">Be unto me a father and a priest.</hi> Though a young man, and taken up at the door, yet, if he take him for a priest, he will respect him as a father, so far is he from setting him among his servants. He asks not for his credentials, takes no time to enquire how he behaved in the place of his last settlement, considers not whether, though he was a Levite, yet he might not be of such a bad character as to be a plague and scandal to his family, but thinks, though he should be ever so great a rake, he might serve for a priest to a graven image, like Jeroboam's priest of the <hi type="italic">lowest of the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.31">1 Kings xii. 31</reference>. No marvel if those who can make any thing serve for a god can also make any thing serve for a priest. 2. A tolerable maintenance. He will allow him <hi type="italic">meat, and drink, and clothes,</hi> a <hi type="italic">double suit,</hi> so the word is in the margin, a better and a worse, one for every day's wear and one for holy days, and ten shekels, about twenty-five shillings, a year for spending money—a poor salary in comparison of what God provided for the Levites that behaved well; but those that forsake God's service will never better themselves, nor find a better master. The ministry is the best calling but the worst trade in the world. <div eID="gen5023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5024" type="x-p"/> III. The Levite's settlement with him (<reference osisRef="Judg.17.11">v. 11</reference>): He was <hi type="italic">content to dwell with the man;</hi> though his work was superstitious and his wages were scandalous, he objected against neither, but thought himself happy that he had lighted on so good a house. Micah, thinking himself holier than any of his neighbours, presumed to consecrate this Levite, <reference osisRef="Judg.17.12">v. 12</reference>. As if his building, furnishing, and endowing this chapel authorized him, not only to appoint the person that should officiate there, but to confer those orders upon him which he had no right to give nor the other to receive. And now he shows him respect as a father and tenderness as a son, and is willing thus to make up the deficiency of the coin he gave him. <div eID="gen5024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5025" type="x-p"/> IV. Micah's satisfaction in this (<reference osisRef="Judg.17.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now know I that the Lord will do me good</hi> (that is, he hoped that his new establishment would gain reputation among his neighbours, which would turn to his advantage, for he would share in the profit of his altar; or, rather, he hoped that God would countenance and bless him in all he put his hand unto) <hi type="italic">because I have a Levite to be my priest.</hi> 1. He thought it was a sign of God's favour to him and his images that he had so opportunely sent a Levite to his door. Thus those who please themselves with their own delusions, if Providence unexpectedly bring any thing to their hands that furthers them in their evil way, are too apt to infer thence that God is pleased with them. 2. He thought now that the error of his priesthood was amended all was well, though he still retained his graven and molten image. Note, Many deceive themselves into a good opinion of their state by a partial reformation. They think they are as good as they should be, because, in some one particular instance, they are not so bad as they have been, as if the correcting of one fault would atone for their persisting in all the rest. 3. He thought the making of a Levite into a priest was a very meritorious act, which really was a presumptuous usurpation, andvery provoking to God. Men's pride, and ignorance, and self-flattery, will undertake, not only to justify, but magnify and sanctify, the most daring impieties and invasions upon the divine prerogatives. With much reason might Micah have said, "Now may I fear that God will curse me, because I have debauched one of his own tribe, and drawn him into the worship of a graven image;" yet for this he hopes God will do him good. 4. He thought that having a Levite in the house with him would of course entitle him to the divine favour. Carnal hearts are apt to build too much upon their external privileges, and to conclude that God will certainly do them good because they are born of godly parents, dwell in praying families, are linked in society with those that are very good, and sit under a lively ministry; whereas all this is but like having a Levite to be their priest, which amounts to no security at all that God will do them good, unless they be good themselves, and make a good use of these advantages.  <chapter eID="Judg.17"/> <div eID="gen5025" type="x-p"/>

entries.3781b0b36e8a14b9a845100cde74c35872cab0f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2411"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 17</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.17.1-Judg.17.4">Jud 17:1-4</reference>. Micah Restoring the Stolen Money to His Mother, She Makes Images.</title> <div sID="gen3253" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2411"/><hi type="bold">1. a man of mount Ephraim--</hi>that is, the mountainous parts of Ephraim. This and the other narratives that follow form a miscellaneous collection, or appendix to the Book of Judges. It belongs to a period when the Hebrew nation was in a greatly disordered and corrupt state. This episode of Micah is connected with <reference osisRef="Judg.1.34">Jud 1:34</reference>. It relates to his foundation of a small sanctuary of his own--a miniature representation of the Shiloh tabernacle--which he stocked with images modelled probably in imitation of the ark and cherubim. Micah and his mother were sincere in their intention to honor God. But their faith was blended with a sad amount of ignorance and delusion. The divisive course they pursued, as well as the will-worship they practised, subjected the perpetrators to the penalty of death. <div eID="gen3253" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3125c041fc14ec1450b2f73c8e32025aed82fe9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2412"/><div sID="gen3254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2412"/><hi type="bold">3. a graven image and a molten image--</hi>The one carved from a block of wood or stone, to be plated over with silver; the other, a figure formed of the solid metal cast into a mould. It is observable, however, that only two hundred shekels were given to the founder. Probably the expense of making two such figures of silver, with their appurtenances (pedestals, bases, &c.), might easily cost, in those days, two hundred shekels, which (at 2 shillings, 4 pence each, is about 23 pounds) would be a sum not adequate to the formation of large statues [Taylor, Fragments]. <div eID="gen3254" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0bc134b4b6c5d848ba2480f34c5200a62d4c871: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2413"/><div sID="gen3255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2413"/><hi type="bold">5. the man Micah had an house of gods--</hi>Hebrew, "a house of God"--a domestic chapel, a private religious establishment of his own.<div eID="gen3255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">an ephod--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Exod.28.6">Ex 28:6</reference>).<div eID="gen3256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">teraphim--</hi>tutelary gods of the household (see <reference osisRef="Gen.31.19">Ge 31:19</reference> and see on <reference osisRef="Gen.31.26">Ge 31:26</reference>).<div eID="gen3257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consecrated one of his sons who became his priest--</hi>The assumption of the priestly office by any one out of the family of Aaron was a direct violation of the divine law (<reference osisRef="Num.3.10">Nu 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.16.17">16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.21.5">De 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.4">He 5:4</reference>). <div eID="gen3258" type="x-p"/>
entries.290ca4557492c3fd22c5023349dca8c2c7501a07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2414"/><div sID="gen3259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2414"/><hi type="bold">6. every man did that which was right in his own eyes--</hi>From want of a settled government, there was no one to call him to account. No punishment followed any crime. <div eID="gen3259" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd70041bb5b67990b8cc2f3183b6df1be251266c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2415"/><div sID="gen3260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2415"/><hi type="bold">7. Beth-lehem-judah--</hi>so called in contradistinction to a town of the same name in Zebulun (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.15">Jos 19:15</reference>).<div eID="gen3260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the family--</hi>that is, tribe.<div eID="gen3261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Judah--</hi>Men of the tribe of Levi might connect themselves, as Aaron did (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.23">Ex 6:23</reference>), by marriage with another tribe; and this young Levite belonged to the tribe of Judah, by his mother's side, which accounts for his being in Beth-lehem, not one of the Levitical cities. <div eID="gen3262" type="x-p"/>
entries.5969e5ffc26446e5c54f866787dfb5c96a4e3700: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2416"/><div sID="gen3263" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2416"/><hi type="bold">8. the man departed ... to sojourn where he could find a place--</hi>A competent provision being secured for every member of the Levitical order, his wandering about showed him to have been a person of a roving disposition or unsettled habits. In the course of his journeying he came to the house of Micah, who, on learning what he was, engaged his permanent services. <div eID="gen3263" type="x-p"/>
entries.3dfd9fdf15fd3801db69052f6dbf00d512f6df75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2417"/><div sID="gen3264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2417"/><hi type="bold">10. Micah said unto him, Dwell with me, and be unto me a father--</hi>a spiritual father, to conduct the religious services of my establishment. He was to receive, in addition to his board, a salary of ten shekels of silver, equal to 25 shillings a year.<div eID="gen3264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a suit of apparel--</hi>not only dress for ordinary use, but vestments suitable for the discharge of his priestly functions. <div eID="gen3265" type="x-p"/>
entries.176dd8c009a9cdef80b8f8318b9ffa020f42c10a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2418"/><div sID="gen3266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2418"/><hi type="bold">12. Micah consecrated the Levite--</hi>Hebrew, "filled his hand." This act of consecration was not less unlawful for Micah to perform than for this Levite to receive (see on <reference osisRef="Judg.18.30">Jud 18:30</reference>). <div eID="gen3266" type="x-p"/>
entries.73b3d42035d70d32200061375fd6baa7ffcca41b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2419"/><div sID="gen3267" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2419"/><hi type="bold">13. Now know I that the Lord will do me good--</hi>The removal of his son, followed by the installation of this Levite into the priestly office, seems to have satisfied his conscience, that by what he deemed the orderly ministrations of religion he would prosper. This expression of his hope evinces the united influence of ignorance and superstition. <chapter eID="Judg.17"/>

entries.8a562fb036eb49b100a6bbe61c29df45f8088c1c: <div eID="gen9105" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen9106" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9107" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9107" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9106" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9108" type="x-p"/> Micah, an Ephraimite, restores to his mother eleven hundred shekels of silver, which he had taken from her, <reference osisRef="Jdg.17.1">Jdg 17:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.17.2">Jdg 17:2</reference>. She dedicates this to God; and out of a part of it makes a graven image and a molten image, and gets them up in the house of Micah, <reference osisRef="Jdg.17.3">Jdg 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.17.4">Jdg 17:4</reference>; who consecrates one of his sons to be his priest, <reference osisRef="Jdg.17.5">Jdg 17:5</reference>. He afterwards finds a Levite, whom he consecrates for a priest, and gives him annually ten shekels of silver, with his food and clothing, <reference osisRef="Jdg.17.6-Jdg.17.13">Jdg 17:6-13</reference>. <div eID="gen9108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9109" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen9109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9110" type="x-p"/> And there was a man of Mount Ephraim - It is extremely difficult to fix the chronology of this and the following transactions. Some think them to be here in their natural order; others, that they happened in the time of Joshua, or immediately after the ancients who outlived Joshua. All that can be said with certainty is this, that they happened when there was no king in Israel; i.e., about the time of the Judges, or in some time of the anarchy, <reference osisRef="Jdg.17.6">Jdg 17:6</reference>.
entries.d90954c895c998357884ae3126e27f3bc564dded: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen9110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9111" type="x-p"/> About which thou cursedst - Houbigant and others understand this of putting the young man to his oath. It is likely that when the mother of Micah missed the money, she poured imprecations on the thief; and that Micah, who had secreted it, hearing this, was alarmed, and restored the money lest the curses should fall on him.
entries.bed84a6220f55a2117ef859cb463bb7be4a62728: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen9111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9112" type="x-p"/> I had wholly dedicated - From this it appears that Micah's mother, though she made a superstitious use of the money, had no idolatrous design, for she expressly says she had dedicated it ליהוה layhovah, to Jehovah; and this appears to have been the reason why she poured imprecations on him who had taken it.
entries.2784fab2750c0e15d6df8a4626eac14cb800bb02: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen9112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9113" type="x-p"/> A graven image and a molten image - What these images were, we cannot positively say; they were most probably some resemblance of matters belonging to the tabernacle. See below.
entries.68b14524a4c56bbafe1e69999f9354d872c8dfaf: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen9113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9114" type="x-p"/> The man Micah had a house of gods - בית אלהים beith Elohim should, I think, be translated house or temple of God; for it is very likely that both the mother and the son intended no more than a private or domestic chapel, in which they proposed to set up the worship of the true God. <div eID="gen9114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9115" type="x-p"/> Made an ephod - Perhaps the whole of this case may be stated thus: Micah built a house of God - a chapel in imitation of the sanctuary; he made a graven image representing the ark, a molten image to represent the mercy-seat, teraphim to represent the cherubim above the mercy-seat, and an ephod in imitation of the sacerdotal garments; and he consecrated one of his sons to be priest. Thus gross idolatry was not the crime of Micah; he only set up in his own house an epitome of the Divine worship as performed at Shiloh. What the teraphim were, see the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.31.19">Gen 31:19</reference>; for the ephod, see the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.25.7">Exo 25:7</reference>; and for the sacerdotal vestments in general, see the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.28.4">Exo 28:4</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen9115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9116" type="x-p"/> Who became his priest - כהן cohen, which the Targum translates chumera. The word כהן cohen is the common name in Hebrew for a priest of the true God; but sometimes it is applied to idolatrous priests. When it is to be understood in the former sense, the Targum renders it cahen; when in the latter, it uses the word כומרא chumera, by which it always understands an idolatrous priest. But that this was not a case of idolatry, and that the true God was worshipped here, is evident from the word Jehovah being used, <reference osisRef="Jdg.17.4">Jdg 17:4</reference>, and oracular answers being given at this house, as we see from <reference osisRef="Jdg.18.6">Jdg 18:6</reference>, etc.
entries.9e8933f3f0784cbdf7b254e5ca9448c2696fa222: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen9116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9117" type="x-p"/> There was no king in Israel - The word מלך melech, which generally means king, is sometimes taken for a supreme governor, judge, magistrate, or ruler of any kind; (see <reference osisRef="Gen.36.31">Gen 36:31</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deu.33.5">Deu 33:5</reference>); and it is likely it should be so understood here. <div eID="gen9117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9118" type="x-p"/> Every man did that which was right in his own eyes - He was his own governor, and what he did he said was right; and, by his cunning and strength, defended his conduct. When a man's own will, passions, and caprice, are to be made the rule of law, society is in a most perilous and ruinous state. Civil government is of God; and without it the earth must soon be desolated. There was a time when there was no king in England; and that was, in general, a time of scandal to religion, and oppression to men.
entries.4c628396967c04cdc50e0636e490330ef8052b2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen9118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9119" type="x-p"/> Of the family of Judah - The word family may be taken here for tribe; or the young man might have been of the tribe of Judah by his mother, and of the tribe of Levi by his father, for he is called here a Levite; and it is probable that he might have officiated at Shiloh, in the Levitical office. A Levite might marry into any other tribe, providing the woman was not an heiress.
entries.504bb9c56f9e6596ebcd78d65ff21296e8a39d67: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen9119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9120" type="x-p"/> To sojourn where he could find - He went about the country seeking for some employment, for the Levites had no inheritance: besides, no secure residence could be found where there was no civil government.
entries.268c5a268f2bec2840943af245bac03c7575d97f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen9120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9121" type="x-p"/> Be unto me a father and a priest - Thou shalt be master of my house, as if thou wert my father; and, as priest, thou shalt appear in the presence of God for me. The term father is often used to express honor and reverence. <div eID="gen9121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9122" type="x-p"/> Ten shekels of silver - About thirty shillings per annum, with board, lodging, and clothes. Very good wages in those early times.
entries.4bc881e63acabb749542386636a388f6ad60d9cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen9122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9123" type="x-p"/> The Levite was content - He thought the place a good one, and the wages respectable.
entries.f170a5f3c1d672e8a66c63909a6de99c6e33f26c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen9123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9124" type="x-p"/> Micah consecrated the Levite - וימלא את יד vayemalle eth yad, he filled his hands, i.e., he gave him an offering to present before the Lord, that he might be accepted by him. He appointed him to be priest; God was to accept and consecrate him; and for this purpose he filled his hand; i.e., furnished him with the proper offering which he was to present on his inauguration.
entries.8b22c4fc72a49fa5d29c6c7c27d8062942dfebef: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen9124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9125" type="x-p"/> Now know I that the Lord will do me good - As he had already provided an epitome of the tabernacle, a model of the ark, mercy-seat, and cherubim; and had got proper sacerdotal vestments, and a Levite to officiate; he took for granted that all was right, and that he should now have the benediction of God. Some think that he expected great gain from the concourse of the people to his temple; but of this there is no evidence in the text. Micah appears to have been perfectly sincere in all that he did. <div eID="gen9125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9126" type="x-p"/> I Have already remarked that there is no positive evidence that Micah or his mother intended to establish any idolatrous worship. Though they acted without any Divine command in what they did; yet they appear, not only to have been perfectly sincere, but also perfectly disinterested. They put themselves to considerable expense to erect this place of worship, and to maintain, at their own proper charges, a priest to officiate there; and without this the place, in all probability, would have been destitute of the worship and knowledge of the true God. His sincerity, disinterestedness, and attachment to the worship of the God of his fathers, are farther seen in the joy which he expressed on finding a Levite who might legally officiate in his house. It is true, he had not a Divine warrant for what he did; but the state of the land, the profligacy of his countrymen, his distance from Shiloh, etc., considered, he appears to deserve more praise than blame, though of the latter he has received a most liberal share from every quarter. This proceeds from that often-noticed propensity in man to take every thing which concerns the character of another by the worst handle. It cannot be considered any particular crime, should these notes be found at any time leaning to the other side.  <chapter eID="Judg.17"/> <div eID="gen9126" type="x-p"/>

entries.057bf5b32895e11b871a97da3a09f2a15b19de11: Jdg 17:1-3 <div eID="gen3456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3457" type="x-p"/> A man of the mountains of Ephraim named Micah (מיכיהוּ, Jdg 17:1, Jdg 17:4, when contracted into מיכה, Jdg 17:5, Jdg 17:8, etc.), who set up this worship for himself, and “respecting whom the Scriptures do not think it worth while to add the name of his father, or to mention the family from which he sprang” (<hi type="italic">Berleb. Bible</hi>), had stolen 1100 shekels of silver (about £135) from his mother. This is very apparent from the words which he spoke to his mother (v. 2): “<hi type="italic">The thousand and hundred shekels of silver which were taken from thee </hi>(the singular לקּח refers to the silver), <hi type="italic">about which thou cursedst and spakest of also in mine ears </hi>(i.e., didst so utter the curse that among others I also heard it), <hi type="italic">behold, this silver is with me; I have taken it.</hi>” אלה, to swear, used to denote a malediction or curse (cf. אלה קול, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.1">Lev 5:1</reference>). He seems to have been impelled to make this confession by the fear of his mother’s curse. But his mother praised him for it, - “<hi type="italic">Blessed be my son of Jehovah,</hi>” - partly because she saw in it a proof that there still existed a germ of the fear of God, but in all probability chiefly because she was about to dedicate the silver to Jehovah; for, when her son had given it back to her, she said (v. 3), “<hi type="italic">I have sanctified the silver to the Lord from my hand for my son, to make an image and molten work.</hi>” The perfect הקדּשׁתּי is not to be taken in the sense of the pluperfect, “I had sanctified it,” but is expressive of an act just performed: I have sanctified it, I declare herewith that I do sanctify it. “<hi type="italic">And now I give it back to thee,</hi>” namely, to appropriate to thy house of God.
entries.0713c988aa903c8ea5665a3b1f413939582933ed: Jdg 17:4 <div eID="gen3457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3458" type="x-p"/> Hereupon-namely, when her son had given her back the silver (“he restored the silver unto his mother” is only a repetition of <hi type="italic">Jdg 17:3</hi>, introduced as a link with which to connect the appropriation of the silver)-the mother took 200 shekels and gave them to the goldsmith, who made an image and molten work of them, which were henceforth in Micah’s house. The 200 shekels were not quite the fifth part of the whole. What she did with the rest is not stated; but from the fact that she dedicated the silver generally, i.e., the whole amount, to Jehovah, according to Jdg 17:3, we may infer that she applied the remainder to the maintenance of the image-worship.<note placement="foot">There is no foundation for <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi>'s opinion, that the 200 shekels were no part of the 1100, but the trespass-money paid by the son when he gave his mother back the money that he had purloined, since, according to <reference osisRef="Lev.6.5">Lev 6:5</reference>, when a thief restored to the owner any stolen property, he was to add the fifth of its value. There is no ground for applying this law to the case before us, simply because the taking of the money by the son is not even described as a theft, whilst the mother really praises her son for his open confession.</note><hi type="italic">Pesel</hi> and <hi type="italic">massecah</hi> (image and molten work) are joined together, as in Deu 27:15. The difference between the two words in this instance is very difficult to determine. <hi type="italic">Pesel</hi> signifies an idolatrous image, whether made of wood or metal. <hi type="italic">Massecah</hi>, on the other hand, signifies a cast, something poured; and when used in the singular, is almost exclusively restricted to the calf cast by Aaron or Jeroboam. It is generally connected with עגל, but it is used in the same sense without this definition (e.g., <reference osisRef="Deut.9.12">Deu 9:12</reference>). This makes the conjecture a very natural one, that the two words together might simply denote a likeness of Jehovah, and, judging from the occurrence at Sinai, a representation of Jehovah in the form of a molten calf. But there is one obstacle in the way of such a conjecture, namely, that in Jdg 18:17-18, <hi type="italic">massecah</hi> is separated from <hi type="italic">pesel</hi>, so as necessarily to suggest the idea of two distinct objects. But as we can hardly suppose that Micah’s mother had two images of Jehovah made, and that Micah had both of them set up in his house of God, no other explanation seems possible than that the <hi type="italic">massecah</hi> was something belonging to the <hi type="italic">pesel</hi>, or image of Jehovah, but yet distinct from it-in other words, that it was the pedestal upon which it stood. The <hi type="italic">pesel</hi> was at any rate the principal thing, as we may clearly infer from the fact that it is placed in the front rank among the four objects of Micah’s sanctuary, which the Danites took with them (Jdg 18:17-18), and that in Jdg 18:30-31, the <hi type="italic">pesel</hi> alone is mentioned in connection with the setting up of the image-worship in Dan. Moreover, there can hardly be any doubt that <hi type="italic">pesel</hi>, as a representation of Jehovah, was an image of a bull, like the golden calf which Aaron had made at Sinai (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.4">Exo 32:4</reference>), and the golden calves which Jeroboam set up in the kingdom of Israel, and one of which was set up in Dan (1Ki 12:29).
entries.861ea07898d6597f29612114faa623004b58ef5b: Jdg 17:5-6 <div eID="gen3458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3459" type="x-p"/> His mother did this, because her son Micah had a house of God, and had had an ephod and teraphim made for himself, and one of his sons consecrated to officiate there as a priest. מיכה האישׁ (the man Micah) is therefore placed at the head absolutely, and is connected with what follows by לו: “<hi type="italic">As for the man Micah, there was to him </hi>(he had) <hi type="italic">a house of God</hi>.” The whole verse is a circumstantial clause explanatory of what precedes, and the following verbs ויּעשׂ, וימלּא, and ויהי, are simply a continuation of the first clause, and therefore to be rendered as pluperfects. Micah’s <hi type="italic">beth</hi> <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> (house of God) was a domestic temple belonging to Micah’s house, according to Jdg 18:15-18. את־יד מלּא, to fill the hand, i.e., to invest with the priesthood, to institute as priest (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.7.37">Lev 7:37</reference>). The <hi type="italic">ephod</hi> was an imitation of the high priest’s shoulder-dress (see at Jdg 8:27). The <hi type="italic">teraphim</hi> were images of household gods, penates, who were worshipped as the givers of earthly prosperity, and as oracles (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.31.19">Gen 31:19</reference>). - In Jdg 17:6 it is observed, in explanation of this unlawful conduct, that at that time there was no king in Israel, and every one did what was right in his own eyes.
entries.001e1ad3f9a6cdac3b08a5d83989e79e4a8e596a: Jdg 17:7-9 <hi type="italic">Appointment of a Levite as Priest</hi>. - Jdg 17:7. In the absence of a Levitical priest, Micah had first of all appointed one of his sons as priest at his sanctuary. He afterwards found a Levite for this service. A young man from Bethlehem in Judah, of the family of Judah, who, being a Levite, stayed (גּר) there (in Bethlehem) as a stranger, left this town to sojourn “<hi type="italic">at the place which he should find,</hi>” sc., as a place that would afford him shelter and support, and came up to the mountains of Ephraim to Micah’s house, “making his journey,” i.e., upon his journey. (On the use of the <hi type="italic">inf. constr</hi>. with ל in the sense of the Latin gerund in <hi type="italic">do</hi>, see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §280, <hi type="italic">d</hi>.) Bethlehem was not a Levitical town. The young Levite from Bethlehem was neither born there nor made a citizen of the place, but simply “sojourned there,” i.e., dwelt there temporarily as a stranger. The further statement as to his descent (<hi type="italic">mishpachath Judah</hi>) is not to be understood as signifying that he was a descendant of some family in the tribe of Judah, but simply that he belonged to the Levites who dwelt in the tribe of Judah, and were reckoned in all civil matters as belonging to that tribe. On the division of the land, it is true that it was only to the priests that dwelling-places were allotted in the inheritance of this tribe (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.9-Josh.21.19">Jos 21:9-19</reference>), whilst the rest of the Levites, even the non-priestly members of the family of Kohath, received their dwelling-places among the other tribes (Jos 21:20.). At the same time, as many of the towns which were allotted to the different tribes remained for a long time in the possession of the Canaanites, and the Israelites did not enter at once into the full and undisputed possession of their inheritance, it might easily so happen that different towns which were allotted to the Levites remained in possession of the Canaanites, and consequently that the Levites were compelled to seek a settlement in other places. It might also happen that individuals among the Levites themselves, who were disinclined to perform the service assigned them by the law, would remove from the Levitical towns and seek some other occupation elsewhere (see also at Jdg 18:30).<note placement="foot">There is no reason, therefore, for pronouncing the words יהוּדה ממּשׁפּחת (of the family of Judah) a gloss, and erasing them from the text, as <hi type="italic">Houbigant</hi> proposes. The omission of them from the <hi type="italic">Cod. Vat</hi>. of the lxx, and from the Syriac, is not enough to warrant this, as they occur in the <hi type="italic">Cod. Al</hi>. of the lxx, and their absence from the authorities mentioned may easily be accounted for from the difficulty which was felt in explaining their meaning. On the other hand, it is impossible to imagine any reason for the interpolation of such a gloss into the text.</note>
entries.a59d4096342d60c06642932f94c94d767c592ac4: Jdg 17:10-13 <div eID="gen3459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3460" type="x-p"/> Micah made this proposal to the Levite: “<hi type="italic">Dwell with me, and become my father and priest; I will give thee ten shekels of silver yearly, and fitting out with clothes and maintenance.</hi>” אב, <hi type="italic">father</hi>, is an honourable title give to a priest as a paternal friend and spiritual adviser, and is also used with reference to prophets in 2Ki 6:21 and 2Ki 13:14, and applied to Joseph in Gen 45:8. ליּמים, <hi type="italic">for the days</hi>, sc., for which a person was engaged, i.e., for the year (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.7">1Sa 27:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lev.25.29">Lev 25:29</reference>). “<hi type="italic">And the Levite went,</hi>” i.e., went to Micah’s house. This meaning is evident from the context. The repetition of the subject, “the Levite,” precludes our connecting it with the following verb ויּואל. - In Jdg 17:11-13 the result is summed up. The Levite resolved (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.1.5">Deu 1:5</reference>) to dwell with Micah, who treated him as one of his sons, and entrusted him with the priesthood at his house of God. And Micah rejoiced that he had got a Levite as priest, and said, “<hi type="italic">Now I know that Jehovah will prosper me.</hi>” This belief, or, to speak more correctly, superstition, for which Micah was very speedily to atone, proves that at that time the tribe of Levi held the position assigned it in the law of Moses; that is to say, that it was regarded as the tribe elected by God for the performance of divine worship. The Image-Worship Removed to Laish-Dan. - Jdg 18:1-10. <hi type="italic">Spies sent out by the tribe of Dan, </hi>to seek for a place suitable for a settlement, and their success.  <chapter eID="Judg.17"/> <div eID="gen3460" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p>AND there was a man <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The things mentioned here, and in the following Chap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters, did not happen in the order in which they are put; but much sooner, even presently after the Death of the Elders that over-lived <ns0:hi>Ioshua, Iudg.</ns0:hi> 2. 7. as appears by divers passa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ges; as First, because the place called <ns0:hi>Mahaneh-Dan,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>the camp of Dan, Iudg.</ns0:hi> 13. 25. was so called from that which was done, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 18. 12. Secondly, Because the <ns0:hi>Danites</ns0:hi> had not yet got all their Inheritance, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 18. 1. which is not credible of them, above 300 Years after <ns0:hi>Ioshuah</ns0:hi>'s Death. Thirdly, because <ns0:hi>Phinehas</ns0:hi> the son of <ns0:hi>Eleazar</ns0:hi> was Priest at this time, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 20. 28. who must have been about 350 years old, if this had been done after <ns0:hi>Sampson</ns0:hi>'s Death, which is more than improbable.</ns0:note> of mount Ephraim, whose name was <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And he said unto his mother, The eleven hundred <ns0:hi>shekels</ns0:hi> of silver that were taken from thee, about which thou cursedst <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Didst Curse the Person who had taken them away, and that in my hearing, as it follows.</ns0:note>, and spakest of also in mine ears, behold, the silver <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> with me, I took <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The fear of thy Curse makes me acknowledge mine Offence, and beg thy Pardon.</ns0:note>. And his mother said, Blessed <ns0:hi>be thou</ns0:hi> of the LORD <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">I willingly consent to, and beg from God the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />moval of the Curse, and a Blessing instead of it. Be thou free from my Curse, because thou hast so honestly restored it.</ns0:note>, my son.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And when he had restored the eleven hun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dred <ns0:hi>shekels</ns0:hi> of silver to his mother, his mother said, I had wholly <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">

Whereby it is apparent, that neither she, nor her Son; intended to forsake the true God or his Worship; as appears from his rejoycing when he had got a Priest of the Lords appointment, of the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Levi, Iudg.</ns0:hi> 17. 13. but onely to Worship God by an Image; which also it is appa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rent, that both the <ns0:hi>Israelites, Exod.</ns0:hi> 32. 1, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ieroboam</ns0:hi> af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terwards, designed to do.</ns0:note>, from my hand, for my son <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either, First, for the honour and benefit of thy self, and Family; that you need not be con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinually going to <ns0:hi>Shiloh</ns0:hi> to Worship, but may do it as well at home by these Images. Or, Secondly, that thou mayest cause these things to be made; to which end, she restored all the Money to him, as it here follows.</ns0:note> to make a graven image, and a molten image <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Many think this was but one Image, partly Graven, and partly Molten. But it seems more probable, that they were two distinct Images, because they are so plainly distinguished, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 18. 17, 18. where also some other words come between them. It is true, <ns0:hi>the graven image</ns0:hi> alone is mentioned, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 18. 20, 30, 31. not exclusively to the other, as appears from what is said just before; but by a common Synecdoche, whereby one is put for all; especially, where that one is esteemed the chief.</ns0:note>: now there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore I will restore it unto thee <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To dispose of, as I say.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Yet he restored the money unto his mother <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Though his Mother allowed him to keep it, yet he per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sisted in his resolution to restore it, that she might dispose of it as she pleased; and did actually restore it, as was said before; and now confirms the former Restitution, and therefore is twice said to <ns0:hi>restore</ns0:hi> it.</ns0:note>, and his mother took two hundred <ns0:hi>shekels</ns0:hi> of silver <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Reserving 900 <ns0:hi>Shekels</ns0:hi> either for the <ns0:hi>Ephod</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Teraphim,</ns0:hi> or for other things re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lating to this Worship: or for her own private use; being, it seems, cooled in her first Zeal, and willing to have as cheap a Religion as she could, as also her Son <ns0:hi>Micah</ns0:hi> was, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 17. 10.</ns0:note>, and gave them to the founder, who made there<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> of <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Made them, either, First, of that Matter: Or, Secondly, for that money.</ns0:note> a graven image, and a molten image, and they were in the house of Micah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And the man Micah had an house of gods <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">

                        </ns0:gap> the hand.</ns0:note> con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />secrated one of his sons, who became his priest <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Because the <ns0:hi>Levites</ns0:hi> in that corrupt Estate of the Church, neglected the Exercise of their Office, and therefore were neglected by the People, and others put into their Employment. But this kind of Priest<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hood was condemned, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 16. 40. and 18. 2, 7.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 18. 1. and 21. 2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> In those days <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> no King <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> No Judge to Govern and Controul them. The word <ns0:hi>King</ns0:hi> being here used largely for a Supreme Magistrate; as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 36. 31. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33. 5. God raised up Judges to Rule and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liver the People, when he saw fit; and at other times for their Sins he suffered them to be without them, and such a time this was; and therefore they ran into that Idolatry, from which the Judges usually kept them; as appears by that solemn and oft-repeated passage in this Book, that after the Death of such or such a Judge, the people forsook the Lord, and turned to Idols.</ns0:note> in Israel, <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> every man did <ns0:hi>that which was</ns0:hi> right in his own eyes <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Not what pleased God, but what best suited his own fancy or lusts.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 ¶ And there was a young man out of Bethle<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hem-Judah <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>of Bethlehem-Iudah,</ns0:hi> so called here, as <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 2. 1, 5. to difference it from <ns0:hi>Bethlehem</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Zebulun, Iosh.</ns0:hi> 19. 15. There he was born and bred.</ns0:note>, of the family of Judah <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of, or belonging to the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah;</ns0:hi> not by Birth, for he was a <ns0:hi>Levite;</ns0:hi> nor by his Mother, for though that might be true, the Mothers-side is not regarded in Genealogies; but by his Habitation and Ministration. For the <ns0:hi>Levites,</ns0:hi> especially in times of Confu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion and Irreligion, were dispersed among all the Tribes; and this mans Lot fell into the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah:</ns0:hi> which seems to be here noted by way of reflection upon that Tribe, and as an evidence of the general defection, that a <ns0:hi>Levite</ns0:hi> could not find entertainment in that great and fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mous Tribe which God had put so much honour upon, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 49. 8, 9, 10, 11. and therefore was forced to wander and seek for subsistence elsewhere.</ns0:note>, who was a Levite, and he sojourned there <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">So he expresseth it, because this was not the proper, nor usual place of his abode, this being no <ns0:hi>Levitical</ns0:hi> City.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And the man departed out of the city from Bethlehem-Judah, to sojourn where he could find <ns0:hi>a place</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">For employment and a lively-hood; for the Tithes and Offerings, which were their maintenance, not being brought in to the house of God, the <ns0:hi>Levites</ns0:hi> and Priests must needs be reduced to great streights.</ns0:note>, and he came to mount Ephraim, to the house of Micah <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />king his way.</ns0:note> as he journeyed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And Micah said unto him, Whence comest thou? and he said unto him, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> a Levite of Beth<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lehem-Judah, and I go to sojourn where I may find <ns0:hi>a place.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And Micah said unto him, Dwell with me, and be unto me a father and a priest <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">For, <ns0:hi>a Father, that is, a Priest,</ns0:hi> a Spiritual Father, a Teacher or Instructor, for such are called <ns0:hi>Fathers;</ns0:hi> see 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 6. 21. and 8. 9. and 13. 14. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 22. 21. He pretends Reverence and Submission to him; and what is wanting in his Wages, he pays him in empty Titles.</ns0:note>, and I will give thee ten <ns0:hi>shekels</ns0:hi> of silver by the year, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, a double <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> an or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />de<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> of gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments.</ns0:note> a suit of apparel, and thy victuals. So the Levite went in.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And the Levite was content <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Being constrained by necessity, and infected with the common contagion of the Superstition and Idolatry of the times.</ns0:note> to dwell with the man, and the young man was unto him as one of his sons <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Treated with the same degree of kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness and affection.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And Micah consecrated the Levite <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To be a Priest, for which he thought a Consecration necessary, as knowing that the <ns0:hi>Levites</ns0:hi> were no less ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cluded from the Priests office than the people.</ns0:note>, and the young man became his priest <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Instead of his Son, whom he had Consecrated for want of a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>it<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. but now seems to restrain him from the exercise of that Office, and to devolve it wholly upon the <ns0:hi>Levite,</ns0:hi> who was nearer akin to it.</ns0:note>, and was in the house of Micah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Then said Micah, Now know I that the LORD will do me good <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">I am assured God will Bless me. So blind and grosly partial he was in his Judgment, to think that one right circumstance would answer for all his substantial errors, in making and worshipping Images against Gods express Command, in worshipping God in a forbidden place; and in that he being an <ns0:hi>Ephraimite</ns0:hi> presumed to make a Priest, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, seeing I have a Levite to <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> priest.</ns0:p>
